newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Postponement eases tensions in Bosnian flashpoint.
newsitem.headline: Postponement eases tensions in Bosnian flashpoint.

text.p: Tensions between Bosnian Serbs and Moslems eased around the northern town of Brcko on Friday after an international arbiter decided to postpone any clear resolution of a territorial dispute.
Moslem refugees from Brcko said they were not happy with the decision but expressed relief that the arbiter had chosen not to hand over Brcko to Serb authorities as many diplomats had predicted.
The refugees had threatened to march into Serb-held territory to reclaim their homes after hearing reports on Thursday that the arbiter might allow Serb authorities to keep the town.

But outrage gave way to confusion on the streets of this tiny village only three km (two miles) from Brcko, as Moslem refugees debated the consequences of the arbiter's decision to place the strategic town under international supervision pending a final ruling on its future next year.
"Nothing's clear to me anymore. We're all now in a big prison," said Muhamad Murukovic, who fled Brcko when it fell to Serb forces in May 1992.
Razim Bjelic said he and other refugees were tired of waiting for foreign powers to determine their fate and accused U.S. diplomats of playing with the lives of ordinary people.
"All this reminds me of an international circus," Bjelic said. "It seems that the international community has been against us since the very beginning."

Several thousand Moslems held a rally in the nearby village of Rahici on Friday afternoon. They heard speeches from Moslem- Croat federation officials who promised them the arbiter's ruling would ensure the return of Brcko refugees.

"This is only one more battle in our struggle for the final decision which is to come. We have to struggle one more year," Sejfudin Zahirovic, a member of the federation arbitration team, told Reuters.
As the deadline for a decision drew closer this month, anxieties rose in the rival Serb and Moslem communities in the Brcko region.

Tensions were already running high in Bosnia with the eruption of violence in the southwest town of Mostar on Monday. Croats opened fire on Moslems trying to visit a cemetery in the bitterly divided town, killing one man.
U.S. Bradley fighting vehicles and tanks rumbled along the roads around Brcko on Friday as the NATO-led peace force put on a show of force to defuse tensions.
Serbs in Brcko, many of whom are refugees from other parts of Bosnia, said delaying a resolution to the dispute carried serious risks.

"This is postponing a huge problem which had to be resolved today. As it is, uncertainty remains and the question is whether the problem of Brcko will be resolved by diplomatic means," said one Serb soldier.

The Serbs, who seized Brcko early in the 1992-1995 Bosnian war, view the Sava river port as a lifeline for their autonomous Serb republic which together with the Moslem-Croat federation makes up Bosnia.

Moslems and Croats formed a majority in Brcko before the Bosnian conflict. Bosnian Serb forces, backed by the Yugoslav army, brutally expelled them and about half the 64,000 population is now comprised of Serb refugees.
Many of the Serbs in Brcko are keenly aware that the Moslems are building up their army with the help of a U.S.-sponsored military aid programme.
They fear the narrow land corridor which links their territory could be cut if NATO troops leave in 1998, opening the way for a possible Moslem offensive.
